title: Every Exchange Surface Has a Cost

scenes.tts: A barley leaf cannot take in C O two without letting water out. The gas enters through tiny pores called stomata. Water vapour leaves through the very same pores. When the stomata are open, both things happen at once.
scenes.caption: A barley leaf cannot take in CO2 without letting water out. The gas enters through tiny pores called stomata. Water vapour leaves through the very same pores. When the stomata are open, both things happen at once.
scenes.visual: Block cross-section of a barley leaf with a waxy layer and one open stoma; green CO2 arrow in, blue water-vapour arrow out through the same gap.
scenes.narration: A barley leaf cannot take in CO2 without letting water out. The gas enters through tiny pores called stomata. Water vapour leaves through the very same pores. When the stomata are open, both things happen at once.

scenes.tts: An adult human lung faces a version of the same bargain. Gas must dissolve in a thin, wet film before it can diffuse into cells. A wet surface in air loses water by evaporation. Every breath carries water away. A stoma can close its gap. The lung sits inside the chest and cannot close.
scenes.visual: Two panels: barley stoma that closes, and nested outlines chest > lung > moist surface with gas in and water vapour out, that stays open.
scenes.narration: An adult human lung faces a version of the same bargain. Gas must dissolve in a thin, wet film before it can diffuse into cells. A wet surface in air loses water by evaporation. Every breath carries water away. A stoma can close its gap. The lung sits inside the chest and cannot close.

scenes.tts: How do we count the cost? Divide the carbon gained by the water lost. This is called water-use efficiency. Here are two made-up leaves, not barley data. Leaf A gains twenty micromoles of C O two and loses five millimoles of water, per square metre per second. Its efficiency is four point zero micromoles of C O two per millimole of water.
scenes.caption: How do we count the cost? Divide the carbon gained by the water lost. This is called water-use efficiency. Here are two made-up leaves, not barley data. Leaf A gains 20 µmol CO2 and loses 5 mmol H2O, per m2 per s. Its efficiency is 4.0 µmol CO2 per mmol H2O.
scenes.visual: The ratio carbon gained over water lost is written; Leaf A bars (green 20, blue 5) give 4.0.
scenes.narration: How do we count the cost? Divide the carbon gained by the water lost. This is called water-use efficiency. Here are two made-up leaves, not barley data. Leaf A gains 20 µmol CO2 and loses 5 mmol H2O, per m2 per s. Its efficiency is 4.0 µmol CO2 per mmol H2O.

scenes.tts: Leaf B has fewer stomata. It gains sixteen and loses three, so its efficiency is five point three. It gains twenty percent less carbon, but loses forty percent less water. Neither leaf is better everywhere. When water is scarce, leaf B keeps more water for each unit of carbon. When water is plentiful and carbon limits growth, leaf A gains more.
scenes.visual: Leaf B bars next to A (16, 3, 5.3); 0.8 and 0.6 of A; two cases, water scarce favours B, carbon limiting favours A.

scenes.tts: You might expect less grain from a leaf with fewer stomata. Researchers tested this in barley. They added extra copies of one barley gene, which limits stomatal development. In the mature sixth leaf, two lines kept about twenty-four percent and twelve percent of the control stomatal density. Gas exchange fell in well-watered plants. With five plants per group, no statistically significant drop in grain yield was seen. That does not prove the yields equal. It means no loss was detected.
scenes.visual: Bars of stomatal density relative to control (100, 24, 12); gas exchange fell; yield: no significant drop, 5 plants per group, not proof of equal.
scenes.narration: You might expect less grain from a leaf with fewer stomata. Researchers tested this in barley. They added extra copies of one barley gene, which limits stomatal development. In the mature sixth leaf, two lines kept about twenty-four percent and twelve percent of the control stomatal density. Gas exchange fell in well-watered plants. With five plants per group, no statistically significant drop in grain yield was seen. That does not prove the yields equal. It means no loss was detected.

scenes.tts: Why does a structure usually fit what it does? Selection acts on inherited variation. A sound claim is that lineages with fewer stomata lost less water and left more descendants in dry places. It is not that the plant made fewer stomata to save water. And the fit is never perfect, because a trade-off links two traits. Improving one worsens the other. Every exchange surface carries a cost.
